## Overview

The Luguru, also known as Rugulu, Lugulu, or Waluguru, are a Bantu, matrilineal ethnic group of Tanzania. They are indigenous to Morogoro District, Mvomero District, and Kilosa District of Morogoro Region, as well as Kibaha District of Pwani Region. They are native to the Uluguru Mountains, which are named after them. In 2001, their population was estimated at about 692,000. The Luguru speak the Bantu Luguru language, also called Kiluguru, which is closely related to Gogo and Zaramo but is not intelligible with other languages. Their folk culture is organized around matrilineal clans and lineages, agricultural production, ancestral rites, initiation, marriage, funerals, house forms, pottery, basketry, and carved insignia.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

They state that Luguru women weave sleeping mats and baskets from wild grass.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Luguru motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Luguru women are described as weaving sleeping mats and baskets from wild grass. Initiation ceremonies involved distinctive temporary forms of presentation. Boys were shaved, anointed, dressed in new clothes, and celebrated with a feast of emergence called *mlao*. After girls’ seclusion, the girl was shaved, anointed, decorated, and carried on the shoulders of young men in ceremonies called *mkole* or *gali-gali*. Participants in ancestral ceremonies put on *lugenge* bracelets.

### Architecture

The majority of the Luguru live in the traditional round house called *msowge*, which is shaped like a beehive. Rectangular *banda*- or *tembe*-type houses are also still constructed in the mountains. Building houses is work performed by both men and women.

A separate ritual structure is the *kibanda cha mizimu*, one hut per matrilineal area constructed specifically for propitiating ancestors.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Luguru women make pottery, while men create tools. Historically, a lack of metal led to the use of the digging stick called *muhaya* and the wooden hoe called *kibode*. The *muhaya* served as a dibble when planting sorghum and millet. Wooden mortars and pestles were used to prepare staple grains.

Each matrilineage possesses insignia that can include a stool called *mkunga*, an axe called *mambaza*, a staff called *tenge*, and a drum. Other insignia are a hat called *fia*, a hatband called *kilemba*, and a wrist-bangle called *mhande*. These insignia are collectively called *mlunga*. In the past, Luguru carvers made ceremonial staves, combs, and other tools with significant artistic value. Hard tools were typically made from bastard ebony because iron was extremely rare. Pool water was collected to make salt.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document wrist adornment and several forms of ritual bodily preparation. Participants in ancestral ceremonies wore *lugenge* bracelets. The matrilineage insignia also included the wrist-bangle called *mhande*.

During the birth ceremony called *kulawa kunzi*, held on the seventh day, the mother and child were shaved, marked with flour, anointed with oil, and given the child’s childhood name. In initiation ceremonies, boys and girls were shaved and anointed; girls were also decorated before being carried after the rites.

## Music & performance

The sources name a drum among the insignia of each matrilineage. They also describe initiation festivities called *ngoma ya tumi* and *kuvunja ungo*, as well as a second feast called *ngoma mwikiro*.

Performance and ceremony are closely connected to social organization. Lineage heads organize major ceremonies to appease ancestral spirits for fertility, rain, protection from misfortune, and other concerns. Clan joking partners called *watani* perform ritual duties during funerals and mortuary ceremonies. The first fruits may be offered at a crossroads or consumed by the lineage head before others in rituals called *kulimbua* or *kuzirula*.

## Dance & theatre

They mention initiation festivities called *ngoma ya tumi* and *kuvunja ungo*, the feast called *ngoma mwikiro*, and the ceremonial carrying of an initiated girl on the shoulders of young men in the rites called *mkole* or *gali-gali*. No choreography, dramatic genre, mask tradition, or theatrical performance is described.

## Festivals & rituals

They do, however, document extensive rituals associated with birth, initiation, marriage, agriculture, religion, and death.

After childbirth, the mother and child were confined for a week. On the seventh day, the ceremony called *kulawa kunzi* involved shaving, flour marking, anointing with oil, and the assignment of the child’s childhood name. Certain foods, including *kunde*, eggs, twin bananas, and pregnant animals, were forbidden to expectant mothers.

Initiation ceremonies were traditionally held for boys and girls. Boys underwent shaving, confinement, and instruction in appropriate sexual behaviour and tribal lore by a specialist called *muhanga*. Their rites could be known as *konghongo*, *kukula*, or *lusona*, and concluded with new names, anointing, new clothes, and the feast of emergence called *mlao*. Girls entered seclusion called *kumbi* a year or longer after their first menstruation. Their ceremonies included *ngoma ya tumi*, *kuvunja ungo*, *ngoma mwikiro*, and the emergence rites called *mkole* or *gali-gali*.

Marriage arrangements commonly involved a go-between called *msenga*. Bridewealth payments included forms called *kifungo*, *ngwale*, or *vilama*, followed by payments called *ngwe*, *mwere*, or *kitangura*. Funeral rites were conducted by *watani*. Mourning lasted seven days, and a small feast called *pombe ya tanga* marked the end of mourning on the eighth day. A week later, *pombe ya kihanza* completed the mortuary rites.

## Foodways

The Luguru are permanent farmers. Hill rice is a staple in the east, while sorghum and maize are important in the west. The sources state that maize was introduced in the 17th century. People in every region also grow vegetables, beans, peas, cassava, bananas, and sweet potatoes. Coffee is grown in some mountainous regions, although it has not been very successful. Fruits and vegetables are produced in significant quantities in the eastern mountain region for export to Dar es Salaam and for residents of the town and estates.

Men and women both farm, but women plant seeds and both harvest. Wooden mortars and pestles are used to prepare staple grains. Women make beer and food. In the western mountains, streams are used for limited irrigation. Luguru have no cattle in the tsetse-free mountains, but keep chickens and a few sheep and goats. Fish are caught with poisons in streams, while hunting is minimal; in the past, small game such as antelope was occasionally hunted, and wood rats and monitor lizards were an important source of protein.

Religious rites may involve food, beer, flour, goats, or chickens. Minor acts of propitiation include scattering food, beer, or flour on graves. In rituals called *kulimbua* or *kuzirula*, the lineage head offers the first fruits at a crossroads or eats some before others. Stored harvests, called *kuhoza*, are accompanied by charms or medicines for protection and purification.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources also record disagreement among accounts of certain burial practices, including whether the body should be flexed. They state that family members may later seek diviners’ advice to determine the circumstances and causes of death. No named narratives or genres are supplied.

## Language & religion

Luguru, also known as *Kiluguru*, is a Bantu language spoken in Morogoro Region and Pwani Region of Tanzania. The name is also spelled Lughuru, Lugulu, or Ruguru. It is closely related to Gogo and Zaramo but is not intelligible with other languages.

Most Luguru are Muslim, while a minority are Christian, and many traditional beliefs and practices remain extant. The Luguru believe in a supreme deity called *mulungu*, but most religious rituals are devoted to ancestral spirits called *wazimu*. These rites, called *kutambika*, are supervised by the matrilineal lineage head, although clan joking partners called *watani* perform some. Rituals take place in sacred groves, where ancestors are interred. Rainmakers and lineage leaders perform rites for fertility, rain, protection, and purification. Beliefs in evil spirits called *shetani* have been introduced by Islamic influence. Diviners provide amulets against bad luck and witchcraft, while medicine bundles called *kago* are scattered in fields to deter crop theft.
